name: WISE 0855-0714
type: Brown dwarf (spectral class Y), the coldest known
summary: WISE 0855-0714 is a brown dwarf: a ball of gas too small to burn like a star. It is the coldest one known, colder than a home freezer, and one of our closest neighbours. It gives off almost no visible light, so it can only be seen in infrared images.
why_interesting: It shines almost only in infrared, which makes it a perfect target for SPHEREx. It is so faint that it barely shows up in a single SPHEREx image. Adding up the images of each visit makes it appear, and then you can watch it move across the sky in a few months.

facts.label: Distance
facts.compare: The fourth-closest known system to the Sun. Measured from its parallax (439.0 ± 2.4 milliarcseconds).

facts.label: Proper motion
facts.compare: In the SPHEREx images, SkyShift sees it move about 3 arcseconds west between November 2025 and April 2026.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.compare: Colder than a home freezer, and much colder than any star. Estimated by fitting models to its light.
facts.source: Zapatero Osorio et al. (2016), A&A 592, A80

facts.label: Infrared brightness (4.0–5.0 µm)
facts.compare: 14 % above the clean NEOWISE W2 value (about 469 µJy, Wright & Foley 2025). The extra light comes from the background star next to it. The older AllWISE value is not used because the 2010 WISE images are contaminated by that source.
facts.source: SkyShift (SPHEREx, detectors D5 and D6); Wright & Foley (2025)

facts.label: Mass
facts.compare: Only a few times heavier than Jupiter. Estimated from models, not measured directly.
facts.source: Zapatero Osorio et al. (2016), A&A 592, A80

facts.label: Size
facts.compare: About the size of Jupiter. This is the radius of the best-fitting model, not a direct measurement.

facts.label: Age
facts.compare: Probably old, but the age is assumed from models, not measured.
facts.source: Zapatero Osorio et al. (2016), A&A 592, A80
